idiom_name: service object (PORO with a single call) or module_function facade, with ActiveRecord::Base.transaction as the unit of work
implementation_notes: Rails' local idiom is the service object: a plain Ruby class named after the use case with a single class-level call that coordinates the fine-grained models, or a module_function set when there is no state to carry - both replace the classic facade class with something smaller, since Ruby needs no interface declaration to make the boundary explicit. The unit of work comes from the framework: ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do ... end commits when the block returns and rolls back when it raises, which is Rails' answer to the container-managed transaction of the J2EE pattern. Keep the explicit service class over scattering the workflow through controller callbacks whenever the same use case is reachable from jobs, API endpoints and the console.
code_sketch:
class Orders::Place < Struct.new(:customer_id, :sku, :qty, keyword_init: true)
  def call                                       # service object = coarse facade
    ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do            # unit of work for the use case
      q = Pricing.quote(sku, qty)
      Inventory.reserve(sku, qty)
      Order.create!(customer_id: customer_id, quote: q)
    end
  end
end
pitfalls: Nested service objects each opening their own transaction turn the inner ones into no-ops or savepoints depending on configuration; make the outer boundary explicit and keep inner calls transaction-neutral.
Returning ActiveRecord models across the facade lets controllers lazy-load associations (N+1 queries over the boundary); return plain values or small DTOs.
Zeitwerk autoloading requires the constant path to match the file path (app/services/orders/place.rb -> Orders::Place); mismatches raise NameError only at call time.
